title: Stealthy GJ-21 Drone Has Launched And Recovered From Type 076 Amphibious Assault Ship, China Claims
summary: China claims its stealthy GJ-21 drone has successfully launched and recovered from a Type 076 amphibious assault ship. If confirmed, this represents a significant milestone in naval airpower, indicating advanced drone integration with non-carrier naval platforms.
detail: China claims its GJ-21 stealth drone successfully launched and recovered from a Type 076 amphibious assault ship. This event, if confirmed, marks a significant leap in China's naval airpower capabilities. Amphibious assault ships are typically designed for helicopter operations or vertical/short take-off and landing aircraft, not fixed-wing drones, especially stealthy ones. The ability to operate advanced unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) from such a platform would greatly expand the People's Liberation Army Navy's (PLAN) operational reach, reconnaissance, and potential strike options without risking human pilots. It suggests the Type 076 class, a new and evolving ship design, is specifically engineered to support advanced drone integration, potentially featuring catapults or other innovative launch/recovery systems. This development could enhance China's power projection in contested regions like the South China Sea and near Taiwan, offering a flexible, survivable, and potentially cost-effective air combat platform that challenges traditional naval airpower doctrines and signals China's rapid progress in both drone technology and naval integration.

title: Highlights From North Korea’s Drone-A-Palooza
summary: North Korea showcased a range of new drone capabilities, including reconnaissance and attack drones, during a recent display. The exhibition also featured a highly aspirational concept for a stealthy Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV).
detail: North Korea recently showcased a range of new drones, including various reconnaissance and attack models, alongside a conceptual design for a stealthy unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV). This display highlights Pyongyang's ongoing commitment to developing its unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology, despite international sanctions. The expansion of its drone arsenal, particularly with potential attack capabilities, could significantly bolster North Korea's intelligence gathering, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities, while also offering new options for asymmetric warfare. While the 'stealthy UCAV concept' is likely aspirational and far from operational, its public display serves as a strategic signal of North Korea's ambition to acquire advanced military technologies. Historically, North Korea has used drones for border incursions and surveillance. The development of more sophisticated, potentially armed drones could complicate regional defense strategies for South Korea, Japan, and U.S. forces, as these systems can be challenging to detect and intercept. This aligns with North Korea's broader strategy of diversifying its military capabilities to deter external threats and project an image of growing technological prowess.

This declaration provides crucial insight into Apple's philosophy regarding AI integration, distinguishing its strategy from competitors who may be rapidly deploying AI features across their product lines. In a tech landscape increasingly dominated by AI hype and rapid development, Apple's stance suggests a deliberate, user-centric approach that prioritizes utility, privacy, and a seamless user experience over simply joining the AI trend. This measured strategy aligns with Apple's historical pattern of refining technologies before widespread implementation, aiming to deliver polished, impactful features rather than superficial additions. It could influence consumer perception, reinforcing Apple's brand image as a provider of thoughtful, high-quality technology solutions.

title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
summary: arXiv:2610.37989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative …
detail: This research introduces GAUSS, a sophisticated simulator designed to predict the performance of Large Language Model (LLM) inference serving. LLM inference, the process of generating responses, is operationally complex due to its two distinct phases—prefill (processing the input prompt) and decode (generating subsequent tokens)—and optimization techniques like continuous batching. Traditional throughput metrics are insufficient for operators who need to provision resources, monitor service quality, and meet strict latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs). GAUSS addresses this by combining calibrated, phase-specific latency models with a queueing model and Monte-Carlo sampling. This allows it to accurately predict full distributions of metrics like time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), as well as sustainable request rates. Crucially, GAUSS can reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware configurations that have not yet been deployed, and it effectively captures critical tail latencies that impact user experience. This capability is vital for optimizing LLM deployments, ensuring cost-effective resource allocation, and maintaining reliable, high-performance AI services in production environments.

title: Context Compaction for World Models
summary: arXiv:2610.38980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at …
detail: This paper tackles a significant challenge in 'world models'—AI systems that build and interact with simulated environments: their inconsistency when revisiting previously generated regions. The authors frame this as a context retrieval problem, drawing parallels to how Large Language Model (LLM) agents manage their internal memory. They introduce a new benchmark specifically designed to measure world model context retrieval, ensuring that results are not skewed by training data recall or nearby frames. Their key contribution is an 'agent harness' that implements context compaction for world models. This technique allows models to effectively retrieve and utilize information from beyond their standard 'context window' (the maximum amount of information they can process at once) without requiring retraining. By enabling more consistent and persistent memory of generated worlds, this research significantly enhances the utility of world models. This is crucial for developing more coherent and realistic AI-driven simulations, games, and potentially future AI assistants that need to maintain a stable understanding of their environment and past interactions over extended periods.

title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
summary: arXiv:2610.39045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done …
detail: This research proposes a framework, 'Arbitrator,' for responsibly integrating AI into critical decision-making processes, specifically focusing on deceased-donor kidney allocation. The core challenge is determining when an AI should make a decision, defer to a human expert, or flag concerning data patterns and deviate from historical practices. In organ allocation, nearly 30% of recovered kidneys are discarded, often because they are difficult to place through the standard waitlist. AI could identify these 'high-risk' kidneys for 'out-of-sequence' (OOS) allocation, potentially saving more lives. However, relying solely on historical data can perpetuate biases or lead to suboptimal outcomes, as past decisions reflect what was done, not necessarily what should have been done. The Arbitrator framework uses data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network to build a system that recommends OOS allocation only when an organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. This approach balances the efficiency gains of AI with the ethical imperative for human oversight, ensuring that AI augments, rather than replaces, human judgment in high-stakes healthcare decisions, fostering trust and maximizing organ utilization.

title: DynaRev: Benchmarking Web Agents under Dynamic Goal Revision
summary: arXiv:2610.40133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated with goals fully specified before execution and fixed thereafter, whereas real users often revise their requirements during interaction. To study such interactions, we introduce DynaRev, a benchmark of 181 tasks to evaluate web agents …
detail: This paper introduces DynaRev, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate 'web agents'—AI systems that interact with websites—under dynamic goal revision. Current benchmarks typically assess agents based on fixed, pre-specified goals, which doesn't reflect real-world user behavior where requirements often change mid-interaction. DynaRev features 181 tasks that incorporate various types of goal revisions (e.g., additive, unconditional overrides, runtime-conditioned overrides), delivered at task-defined 'semantic milestones.' It evaluates agents on correctness, responsiveness, and efficiency using 'trajectory-grounded evaluation,' which assesses the actual steps taken by the agent. Initial evaluations reveal that existing web agents struggle significantly with dynamic revisions, often only partially fulfilling the updated requirements. This highlights a critical gap in current AI capabilities. DynaRev provides an essential tool for researchers and developers to build and test more robust and adaptable web agents. Such agents are crucial for creating truly intelligent digital assistants that can handle the fluid and evolving nature of human-computer interaction, thereby enhancing their practical utility and user experience in complex web-based tasks.

title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
summary: arXiv:2610.40246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be …
detail: This research introduces EnvOS, a framework for rigorously auditing 'computer-use agents'—Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that interact with software—in dynamic environments where information can change mid-task. A significant challenge for these agents is 'stale information,' where a value they've seen becomes outdated before they act on it. EnvOS addresses this by providing a method to build and certify environments that accurately simulate such changes, ensuring that environmental updates fire correctly, tasks remain solvable, and grading is precise. The framework also includes mechanisms to re-check evaluation verdicts using archived evidence. Applying EnvOS to scenarios like clinic booking and insurance claim approval, the study demonstrates that agents like Claude Opus 5 perform poorly when encountering stale information unless the updated value is explicitly shown. Simply reminding the agent to re-check is less effective. This work is crucial for developing reliable and safe AI agents, as it provides a robust methodology to test their resilience against real-world dynamism. Understanding these limitations helps design better strategies for agents to handle evolving information, making them more trustworthy for practical applications.
